items.title: [FEATURE] Advanced Analytics and Reporting with ML
Add langsmith_bulk_export_destination + langsmith_bulk_export resources (bulk export to S3-compatible storage)
items.body:
### Summary

Add two Terraform resources to manage **bulk exports**: `langsmith_bulk_export_destination` (the S3-compatible bucket + credentials a workspace exports to) and `langsmith_bulk_export` (the scheduled export job itself). Backing API is stable and already shipped in self-hosted; thin CRUD wrappers in the style of `langsmith_alert_rule` / `langsmith_workspace_secret`.

Opening as a proposal first per CONTRIBUTING and happy to implement and PR once the shape is agreed, in particular the delete semantics (see call-outs, the API exposes no DELETE for either object).

### Motivation

Bulk export is the supported way to get traces out of LangSmith into a warehouse, and on self-hosted it is per-workspace infrastructure: a bucket, a credential, and one recurring job per tracing project.

Today we (Pigment) bootstrap it with an in-house Python job that GET and POST if necessary on `/api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations` and `/api/v1/bulk-exports` on every deploy, re-listing both collections to stay idempotent. The result is one bucket credential and one export schedule that live outside state, drift silently, and cannot be reviewed in a plan. We would prefer to converge on the provider.

### Backing API (already present)

Workspace-scoped via the provider's configured workspace (`X-Tenant-ID` / `LANGSMITH_WORKSPACE_ID`); both objects carry a server-assigned `id` (uuid).

**Destinations**

| Operation | Method + path | Body |
|---|---|---|
| List | `GET /api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations` | → `BulkExportDestination[]` |
| Read | `GET /api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations/{destination_id}` | → `BulkExportDestination` |
| Create | `POST /api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations` | `BulkExportDestinationCreate`: `{ display_name (req), config (req), destination_type?, credentials? }` |
| Update | `PATCH /api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations/{destination_id}` | `BulkExportDestinationUpdate`: `{ credentials (req) }` — **credentials only** |
| Delete | — | **no endpoint** |

```jsonc
// BulkExportDestinationCreate
{
  "destination_type": "s3",              // enum: "s3"                  (default "s3")
  "display_name":     "string",          // required, pattern ^[a-zA-Z0-9\-_ ']+$
  "config":           BulkExportDestinationS3Config,   // required
  "credentials":      BulkExportDestinationS3Credentials | null
}

// BulkExportDestinationS3Config
{
  "bucket_name":              "string" | null,   // 3..63
  "prefix":                   "string",          // <=2048              (default "")
  "region":                   "string" | null,
  "endpoint_url":             "string" | null,   // <=2048
  "aws_role_arn":             "string" | null,   // assumed instead of static creds
  "include_bucket_in_prefix": true,              // default true; false when the bucket is already in endpoint_url
  "s3_additional_kwargs":     { }      | null,
  "config_kwargs_s3":         { "addressing_style": "virtual" | "path" } | null
}

// BulkExportDestinationS3Credentials  — write-only
{
  "access_key_id":     "string",        // required, 1..255
  "secret_access_key": "string",        // required, 1..2048
  "session_token":     "string" | null  // <=2048
}

// BulkExportDestination  (response) = Create minus `credentials`, plus:
{
  "id": "uuid", "tenant_id": "uuid",
  "created_at": "date-time", "updated_at": "date-time",
  "credentials_keys": ["string"]        // names only — secrets never read back
}

// BulkExportDestinationUpdate  — the ONLY mutable field
{ "credentials": BulkExportDestinationS3Credentials }  // required
```
**Exports**

| Operation | Method + path | Body |
|---|---|---|
| List | `GET /api/v1/bulk-exports?limit=&offset=` | → `BulkExport[]` |
| Read | `GET /api/v1/bulk-exports/{bulk_export_id}` | → `BulkExport` |
| Create | `POST /api/v1/bulk-exports` | `BulkExportCreate`: `{ bulk_export_destination_id (req), start_time (req), session_id?, all_experiments?, end_time?, filter?, format?, format_version?, compression?, interval_hours?, export_fields? }` |
| Update | `PATCH /api/v1/bulk-exports/{bulk_export_id}` | `BulkExportUpdate`: `{ status }` where `BulkExportUpdatableStatus` is the single value `Cancelled` |
| Delete | — | **no endpoint** (cancel is the terminal operation) |

```jsonc
// BulkExportCreate
{
  "bulk_export_destination_id": "uuid",             // required
  "start_time":                 "date-time",        // required
  "session_id":                 "uuid" | null,      // tracing project to export
  "all_experiments":            false,              // default false
  "end_time":                   "date-time" | null, // omit for an open-ended schedule
  "filter":                     "string" | null,
  "format":                     "Parquet",                    // default "Parquet"
  "format_version":             "v1" | "v2_beta",             // default "v1"
  "compression":                "none" | "gzip" | "snappy" | "zstandard",  // default "gzip"
  "interval_hours":             24 | null,          // null = one-shot
  "export_fields":              ["string"] | null
}

// BulkExport  (response) = Create, plus:
{
  "id": "uuid", "tenant_id": "uuid",
  "status": "Created" | "IntervalScheduled" | "Running"
          | "Completed" | "Cancelled" | "Failed" | "TimedOut",
  "created_at": "date-time", "updated_at": "date-time",
  "finished_at": "date-time" | null,
  "source_bulk_export_id": "uuid" | null
}

// BulkExportUpdate  — the ONLY mutable field
{ "status": "Cancelled" }   // BulkExportUpdatableStatus has exactly one value
```

### Proposed resource shape

```hcl
# S3-compatible destination — here a GCS bucket via the XML API + HMAC keys
resource "langsmith_bulk_export_destination" "warehouse" {
  display_name     = "gcs-warehouse-export"
  destination_type = "s3"

  config {
    bucket_name  = "langsmith-traces-eu"
    prefix       = "langsmith-export"
    endpoint_url = "https://storage.googleapis.com"
    region       = "europe-west1"
  }

  credentials {
    access_key_id     = var.hmac_access_key_id
    secret_access_key = var.hmac_secret
  }
}

# Daily recurring export of one tracing project
resource "langsmith_bulk_export" "traces_daily" {
  bulk_export_destination_id = langsmith_bulk_export_destination.warehouse.id
  session_id                 = data.langsmith_project.traces.id

  start_time     = "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"
  interval_hours = 24
  format_version = "v2_beta"
  compression    = "snappy"
}
```

- Resource ID = server `id` for both. Import: `terraform import langsmith_bulk_export.traces_daily <uuid>`.
- `credentials` is `Sensitive` + `WriteOnly`; drift on it is undetectable by design (the API returns only `credentials_keys`), so state keeps what was configured and `credentials_keys` is exposed as a computed attribute.
- `session_id` and `all_experiments` are mutually exclusive in practice — `ConflictsWith`.
- Everything on `langsmith_bulk_export` except `status` is create-only → `RequiresReplace` on `bulk_export_destination_id`, `session_id`, `start_time`, `end_time`, `filter`, `format*`, `compression`, `interval_hours`, `export_fields`. Same for `display_name` and `config` on the destination, since `PATCH` accepts credentials only.
- `session_id` pairs with the existing `langsmith_project` data source, so an export can reference a project by name.

### Notes / call-outs

- **Neither object is deletable via the API.** This is the one thing worth agreeing on before I write Go. For `langsmith_bulk_export`, `Delete` can `PATCH {"status": "Cancelled"}` — that stops the schedule and is a reasonable destroy. For `langsmith_bulk_export_destination` there is no cancel and no delete: `Delete` would have to drop the resource from state and leave the destination on the server, which then silently collides on the next `apply` if `display_name` is unique server-side. 
Options I see, with (c) being the cleanest if a delete endpoint is on the roadmap :
  - (a) remove-from-state + prominent doc warning 
  - (b) `Delete` returns an error directing the user to `terraform state rm`
  -  (c) add `DELETE /api/v1/bulk-exports/destinations/{id}` API-side and have the provider use it. 
- Because `RequiresReplace` on an undeletable destination means create-new-then-orphan-old, the practical impact of the above is not just cosmetic; a `config` change leaves a stale destination behind each time.
- A `Cancelled` export cannot be resumed. If the object is later mutated out-of-band into a terminal state (`Cancelled`, `Failed`, `TimedOut`), `Read` should probably surface it as drift rather than silently removing the resource from state. Open to the maintainers' preference on this.
- `include_bucket_in_prefix` and `config_kwargs_s3.addressing_style` exist specifically for S3-compatible non-AWS backends (GCS, Volcengine TOS). Worth exposing rather than hardcoding AWS assumptions, since self-hosted deployments are the main consumer of bulk export.
- `format` currently has one enum value (`Parquet`); exposing it as an optional attribute anyway keeps the resource forward-compatible.

### Willing to implement

Yes: we have a working reference implementation of the create/list/read calls for both objects; will follow the `alert_rule` resource + acceptance-test + docs/example pattern. Seeking agreement on the destination delete semantics above, and on whether `config`/`credentials` should be nested blocks (as sketched) or flattened onto the resource.

items.title: Add Table Partitioning Option for PostgreSQL

labels.name: community
labels.description: A PR, or an issue with a PR, from a community member

items.body:
## Feature

### Feature description
[Table partitioning](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/11/ddl-partitioning.html) has existed since PostgreSQL 9, but in PostgreSQL 11 has been made significantly easier to use and more performant. 

### Who will this benefit?
Anyone who has solid Medium-Sized™ data that doesn't quite need the complexity or resources provided by BigQuery/RedShift/Snowflake.

For instance, in our current environment we have a table for all email messages sent to every user historically that is 200 million rows. While queryable, it could definitely benefit from using a `range` partition based on dates or even user groups.

items.title: [Spec] Blueprint §33-§35 + §XII Layer 8: Data Moat strategy — 35 schemas longitudinal telemetry, vector embeddings, event log

labels.name: spec
labels.description: Spec-driven issue derived from engineering-spec-v1.0 or Blueprint v1.8

items.body:
## Frontmatter

---
owner: platform
depends_on: [21, 33, 41, 19]
blocks: []
spec_sections: ["section-4.1", "section-4.2", "section-4.3", "patch-1.7"]
blueprint_sections: ["section-33", "section-34", "section-35"]
maturity_target: lender_ready
acceptance:
  - All 35 schema categories implemented in PostgreSQL with correct domain grouping: schemas 1-25 (readiness), 26-30 (credit), 31-35 (BAI-powered)
  - Schemas 31-35 confirmed operational: lender_intelligence_realtime (BLIN), industry_benchmarks (BII), macro_market_indicators (BMS), predicted_funding_outcomes (BPFS), personalization_features (ML feature store)
  - Event log schema implemented: every score change, module completion, coaching interaction, document upload, and funding outcome recorded with timestamp, tenant_id, user_id, event_type, and payload
  - Audit log schema implemented: every admin action, data access by advisor, bureau pull consent, and data deletion request recorded with actor, target, action, and timestamp
  - Vector embeddings pipeline: business profile and coaching interaction summaries embedded via OpenAI embeddings and stored in Pinecone/Weaviate for similar-business case study retrieval
  - Snowflake ETL pipeline (dbt) ingests all 35 schema tables on a daily schedule for long-term warehouse analytics
  - Data compounding proof: a platform-level report demonstrates that BPFS accuracy improves as funded outcome records accumulate (measurable moat evidence)
  - Cross-tenant aggregation guardrails: tenant data used for aggregate ML training only with appropriate anonymization; no cross-tenant PII leakage
  - Data retention lifecycle enforced per §4.4: PII purged at 7 years post-last-activity or on verified deletion request
---

## Details

Implements the Data Moat strategy from Blueprint v1.8 §33 (The Closed Loop Only Bankable Owns), §34 (35 Data Schemas), and §35 (9 Moat-Forming Schemas), plus Layer 8 of the 12-Layer Architecture (Data Layer).

Per Blueprint v1.8 §35: The closed loop only BANKABLE owns: Credit Position -> Cash Flow Intelligence -> Lender Match -> Capital Outcomes. Banks have credit but no cash flow. Plaid has cash flow but no credit. Credit repair shops have credit but no lender match. Lender matchmakers have lender data but no credit position. Bankable has all four.

The 9 moat-forming schemas (§35):
1. bankability_scores (longitudinal score history per business)
2. credit_positions (tri-bureau + business credit longitudinal)
3. cash_flow_telemetry (Plaid-fed transaction and pattern data)
4. lender_outcomes (funded outcomes, terms, approval/denial history)
5. lender_intelligence_realtime (BLIN - actual lender underwriting behavior)
6. industry_benchmarks (BII - industry-adjusted norms)
7. macro_market_indicators (BMS - rate environment, credit cycle signals)
8. predicted_funding_outcomes (BPFS - per-business per-lender approval probability)
9. personalization_features (ML feature store for adaptive intelligence)

The moat compounds because every new funded outcome makes BPFS more accurate, every new lender outcome improves BLIN, and every new industry cohort improves BII. The data advantage grows with scale in a way competitors cannot replicate without years of similar transaction volume.

References: Blueprint v1.8 §33 Data Moat, §34 35 Data Schemas, §35 9 Moat-Forming Schemas, §XII Layer 8 Data Layer, Spec Patch 1.7, engineering-spec-v1.0.html §4.1, §4.2

items.title: Epic: Wall-time observability — bucketed per-step timing + cross-run aggregation
items.body:
## Goal

Make Mantis self-aware about where wall time goes. Today every run reports a single ``total_time_s`` (and a ``cost_breakdown`` for dollars), but no equivalent breakdown for time. Operators / plan authors / model-eval folks can't tell whether a 240s run was bottlenecked by Claude extract, Holo3 inference, Chrome load, or runner overhead — and so can't tell where to optimize.

Build a **bucket-classified wall-time meter** alongside the existing ``CostMeter``, surface it on every ``/v1/predict`` result, and persist it to a queryable store so we can answer "across the last 100 runs of workflow X, what's the p95 latency per bucket and which bucket regressed since last month."

## Why

Three concrete unlocks:

1. **Plan-author feedback.** Today a plan author who wants a 4-min run knows it took 9 min but doesn't know why. With bucketed timing they can see "you have 12 ``extract_data`` steps at 8s each — try a single batch extract." Closes the feedback loop the cost meter already has on $.
2. **Model A/B testing.** When evaluating Holo3-Q5 vs Q8 vs Gemma4-CUA, the answer "Q5 is 22% faster end-to-end" is almost meaningless — the brain might only be 30% of wall time. Bucketed timing lets us compare ``think`` latency in isolation.
3. **Regression detection.** Bucket-level p95 across the last 100 runs of a workflow shows when proxy CONNECT latency spikes, when a Cloudflare bypass adds 10s/run, when a new step type drags ``settle`` up by 2x. Without persistence we can't see this; Prometheus is real-time only and would explode cardinality if labeled by ``workflow_id``.

## What exists today (and the gaps)

- **``CostMeter``** (``gym/cost_meter.py:53``) — tracks ``gpu_seconds`` / ``claude_extract`` count / ``claude_grounding`` count / ``proxy_mb`` → maps to USD. Owns the right shape for time too but only emits dollars.
- **``RUN_DURATION_SECONDS`` histogram** (``metrics.py:118``) — per-run total, no breakdown.
- **``STEP_LATENCY_SECONDS`` histogram** (``metrics.py:212``) — **declared with bucket vocabulary ``(perceive|think|act|settle)`` but never emitted from anywhere in the codebase.** Schema landed, implementation didn't.
- **``StepResult.steps_used``** / **``inference_time``** (``gym/runner.py:1034``) — partial per-step timing, scattered.
- **``build_micro_result``** (``server_utils.py:408``) — returns ``total_time_s`` and per-step ``steps_used``, no time breakdown.

The cost-meter pattern is the model. This epic builds the time-meter twin.

## Scope (3 phases)

### Phase A — ``TimeMeter`` + per-step bucket capture

- [ ] **[#363](#)** — sibling to ``CostMeter``: ``gym/time_meter.py`` with ``record_phase(bucket, seconds)`` and ``totals() -> dict[bucket, seconds]``. Buckets (initial): ``perceive`` (screenshot capture), ``think`` (brain inference), ``act`` (env.step + xdotool), ``settle`` (post-action wait), ``claude_ground`` (grounding refinement), ``claude_extract`` (extract_data calls), ``claude_verify`` (gate / dynamic_verifier), ``load`` (navigate + CF / proxy wait), ``overhead`` (runner / dispatch / Python). Wire from ``MicroPlanRunner`` step handlers and ``GymRunner`` action loop. Emit the existing ``STEP_LATENCY_SECONDS`` histogram per bucket.

### Phase B — Result envelope + telemetry surface

- [ ] **[#365](#)** — add ``wall_time_breakdown: {bucket: seconds}`` to ``build_micro_result`` and ``step_details[].time_breakdown`` per-step. Surface via the existing ``/v1/predict`` ``action=result`` path; same envelope on the Modal HTTP endpoint (#347). No new endpoint needed. Docs page: ``api.md`` adds a "Wall-time breakdown" section with the bucket table.

### Phase C — Durable per-run store + cross-run aggregation

- [ ] **[#366](#)** — write one JSONL line per terminal run to ``$MANTIS_DATA_DIR/runs_log/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl`` carrying ``(run_id, tenant_id, profile_id, workflow_id, model, total_time_s, wall_time_breakdown, cost_breakdown, status, finished_at)``. Query via DuckDB over the JSONL (read-only, no schema migration). Ship a CLI: ``mantis runs stats <workflow_id> [--last N] [--bucket think|extract|...]`` returning p50/p95/p99 per bucket. Optional Phase 2: a minimal markdown report generated weekly into ``$MANTIS_DATA_DIR/reports/``.

## Why durable store on top of Prometheus

Prometheus is for **real-time alerting** — "alert when run-failure rate >5% in last 5 min." It's the wrong tool for **historical / per-workflow analytics** because:

- Cardinality: labeling ``STEP_LATENCY_SECONDS`` by ``workflow_id`` blows up the metric (one series per workflow × bucket × tenant — easily 10k+ series at modest scale).
- Retention: most Prom setups keep 2 weeks of data; we want to look at "this workflow last quarter."
- Query model: Prom's PromQL is great for sliding-window stats, mediocre for "p95 over the last 100 *individual* runs of this exact workflow."

JSONL + DuckDB on the Modal Volume is the cheap and right path: durable, queryable, no infra to host, scales to millions of rows before we'd outgrow it.

## Out of scope

- **Per-action timing inside a single ``env.step``** (xdotool keystroke timing). Out — too fine-grained, adds cost capture overhead.
- **External Postgres / data warehouse export.** If JSONL outgrows DuckDB, replace the backend behind the ``mantis runs stats`` CLI; not now.
- **A web dashboard.** Markdown report is enough until someone asks for HTML.
- **GPU-side timing breakdowns** (which Holo3 layer took longest). Brain-internal, not runner-observable.

## Acceptance criteria (epic-level)

- [ ] Phase A merged: ``TimeMeter`` captures per-step bucketed timing; ``STEP_LATENCY_SECONDS`` actually emits.
- [ ] Phase B merged: every ``/v1/predict`` result carries ``wall_time_breakdown``; both Baseten and Modal endpoints.
- [ ] Phase C merged: ``mantis runs stats <workflow_id>`` returns p50/p95 per bucket from on-disk JSONL.
- [ ] Docs: ``api.md`` has a Wall-time breakdown section; ``operations/`` has a "Reading the time meter" page explaining what each bucket means and which step types contribute to each.
- [ ] One concrete win demonstrated: a plan in the corpus optimized by ≥20% wall time after reading the breakdown for the first time.

## References

- ``src/mantis_agent/gym/cost_meter.py:53`` — pattern to mirror
- ``src/mantis_agent/metrics.py:212`` — ``STEP_LATENCY_SECONDS`` already declared, ready to emit
- ``src/mantis_agent/server_utils.py:408`` — ``build_micro_result``, the envelope to extend
- #74 — ``step_callback`` (per-step hook) — TimeMeter records can flow through this surface
- #346/#347 — recent work that confirmed the envelope round-trips cleanly between Baseten and Modal

items.title: Financial & revenue analytics

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

There is no revenue reporting in the platform. MediCore billing emits `ChargeCaptured`, `InvoiceIssued`, `PaymentReceived`, `RefundIssued` and `ClaimStatusChanged`, and these events settle correctly into the operational ledger, but nothing aggregates them. A hospital finance controller who needs this month's gross revenue by service line, the cash-versus-TPA payer split, receivables ageing, or the claim denial rate has to export raw invoice tables and rebuild the analysis in Excel every month.

This matters on three fronts. Operationally, TPA and government-scheme receivables are where hospitals lose money: a claim rejected on a documentation defect and not chased within the payer's resubmission window becomes an unrecoverable write-off, and without ageing and denial-reason reporting nobody sees the pattern until the quarter closes. Commercially, the finance controller and hospital administrator are the economic buyers of AdminConnect and revenue visibility is the capability they evaluate first. Legally, India's GST regime requires correct HSN/SAC classification and slab treatment, with e-invoicing obligations above the applicable turnover threshold — finance needs a tax view that reconciles to what was actually reported, not an approximation.

Unlike clinical analytics, financial figures cannot be approximate or de-identified into uselessness. A revenue dashboard that disagrees with the billing ledger is worse than no dashboard, because it will be used in board reporting. Reconciliation to the operational ledger is therefore the central engineering requirement, while the OLTP/OLAP separation rule (BRIEF §7) still forbids running these aggregations against the live clinical database.

Affected roles: finance controller, billing manager, TPA co-ordinator, hospital administrator, and the platform's own subscription/finance team.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** hospital finance controller
**I want** revenue, payer-mix, receivables-ageing and denial analytics that reconcile exactly to the billing ledger
**So that** I can close the month from AdminConnect and act on ageing and denial trends before receivables become unrecoverable.

### Scope

**In scope**

* Financial fact and dimension tables in the analytics warehouse, fed from billing domain events with an idempotent Go consumer.
* Metrics: gross and net revenue, revenue by service line and department, payer mix, collection efficiency, average realisation per bed-day, discount and write-off totals.
* Receivables ageing buckets (0–30 / 31–60 / 61–90 / 90+ days) split by payer and payer type (cash, TPA, corporate, government scheme).
* Claim denial analytics: denial rate, denial reason distribution, resubmission outcome, and days-to-settlement.
* A GST view: taxable value, tax by slab and HSN/SAC code, per facility GSTIN and per return period.
* A daily reconciliation job that compares warehouse totals to the operational ledger and raises an alert on any variance.
* AdminConnect dashboard with drill-down from summary tile to contributing invoice list.
* OpenFGA authorisation restricting financial data to finance and administrator roles, scoped per facility.

**Out of scope**

* Clinical quality indicators — owned by #384.
* Bed occupancy and capacity utilisation, including revenue-per-available-bed-day denominators sourced from #386.
* Claim submission, adjudication and resubmission workflow itself — that is the Revenue Cycle epic; this issue reports on it.
* GST return filing or e-invoice IRN generation — owned by the Billing & Tax epic; this issue reports the figures those systems produce.
* Platform subscription revenue and MRR reporting, which is tenant-billing, not hospital-billing.

---

## Recommended Solution

An `revenue-analytics` Go module consumes a durable JetStream pull consumer on `medicore.billing.*` and `medicore.claim.*` and writes into the analytics PostgreSQL 16 cluster. Financial facts are tenant-identifiable by necessity, so RLS on `tenant_id` plus facility-scoped OpenFGA checks carry the whole isolation burden here — there is no pseudonymisation to fall back on. Patient identity is still excluded: facts carry `encounter_id` and `invoice_id`, never patient name, ABHA number or contact details.

**Data model:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_invoice_line (
  line_key        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  facility_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  invoice_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  encounter_id    uuid,
  issued_date_key int  NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_date,
  service_line_key int NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_service_line,
  payer_key       int  NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_payer,
  hsn_sac_code    text NOT NULL,
  gst_rate_bp     int  NOT NULL,              -- basis points, avoids float drift
  gross_amount_paise  bigint NOT NULL,        -- integer minor units only
  discount_paise      bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  taxable_paise       bigint NOT NULL,
  tax_paise           bigint NOT NULL,
  net_amount_paise    bigint NOT NULL,
  source_event_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  CONSTRAINT net_consistent CHECK (net_amount_paise = taxable_paise + tax_paise)
);

CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_receivable_snapshot (
  snapshot_date_key int NOT NULL,
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, facility_id uuid NOT NULL,
  payer_key int NOT NULL, ageing_bucket text NOT NULL,
  outstanding_paise bigint NOT NULL, invoice_count int NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_date_key, tenant_id, facility_id, payer_key, ageing_bucket)
);

CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_claim_event (
  claim_event_key bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, facility_id uuid NOT NULL,
  claim_id uuid NOT NULL, payer_key int NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN
    ('submitted','queried','denied','partially_settled','settled','written_off')),
  denial_reason_code text, claimed_paise bigint, settled_paise bigint,
  event_at timestamptz NOT NULL, source_event_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
```

All money is `bigint` paise. Floating-point currency in a system used for board reporting is a defect waiting to happen, and the `net_consistent` check catches ingestion bugs at write time rather than in a quarterly variance.

Receivables ageing is a **daily snapshot**, not a computed-on-read query. Ageing as at a past date cannot be reconstructed from current invoice state once payments land, and finance needs to reproduce last month's ageing exactly. A Temporal scheduled workflow writes one snapshot per facility per day.

**Reconciliation.** A second Temporal workflow runs after each nightly load, calls MediCore billing's `GET /internal/v1/billing/control-totals?date=&facility_id=` (a read-only endpoint returning invoice count and net total for the period), and compares to the warehouse. Any variance beyond zero writes `analytics.reconciliation_exception` and publishes `AnalyticsReconciliationFailed`, which pages the data team and stamps the dashboard with an "unreconciled" banner. The dashboard must never present unreconciled financials as authoritative.

**API surface:**

* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/summary?from=&to=&facility_id=`
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/by-dimension?dimension=service_line|payer|department&from=&to=`
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/receivables-ageing?as_of=&payer_type=`
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/denials?from=&to=&group_by=reason|payer`
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/gst-summary?period=&gstin=`
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/revenue/drilldown?metric=&period=&dimension_key=` — contributing invoice list, paginated.
* `POST /api/v1/analytics/revenue/exports` — CSV/XLSX job returning a signed time-limited URL.

**Events consumed:** `ChargeCaptured`, `InvoiceIssued`, `InvoiceVoided`, `PaymentReceived`, `RefundIssued`, `ClaimSubmitted`, `ClaimStatusChanged`, `WriteOffApproved`. **Published:** `AnalyticsReconciliationFailed`, `AnalyticsExportRequested`.

**OpenFGA:**

```
type financial_report
  relations
    define facility: [facility]
    define viewer: finance_controller from facility
                 or billing_manager from facility
                 or hospital_admin from facility
    define viewer_all_facilities: group_finance from tenant
    define exporter: finance_controller from facility
```

Clinical roles get no relation at all — a consultant must not read facility revenue. Export is a narrower relation than view, because an exported receivables file leaving the platform is a distinct risk.

**Sequencing.** Depends on the Data Platform epic (warehouse, JetStream retention), on the Billing & Tax epic emitting HSN/SAC and GST rate on invoice-line events, and on a stable payer master in the Revenue Cycle epic. Share `analytics.dim_date` and `dim_facility` with #384 rather than duplicating them.

**Risks.** Invoice voids and credit notes arriving after a period closes will silently restate a reported month — handle by never mutating a closed period in place, instead posting a dated adjustment row and showing restatements explicitly. Payer master churn breaks trend continuity — `dim_payer` is a slowly-changing dimension keyed on surrogate `payer_key` so historical rows keep their original payer attributes. Currency and rounding drift is contained by integer paise plus the write-time check constraint.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a tenant with a closed prior month of billing events across two facilities
**When** the finance controller opens the revenue dashboard for that month and drills from the gross revenue tile into the Radiology service line
**Then** the summary total equals the operational billing ledger's control total to the paise, the payer-mix split sums to the gross total, the drill-down lists the contributing invoices with pagination, and the period is stamped "reconciled" with the reconciliation run timestamp.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the nightly reconciliation detected a ₹4,200 variance between warehouse and ledger net revenue for one facility
**When** any user requests revenue figures covering that facility and date
**Then** the API returns the figures annotated with `reconciled: false` and the variance amount, the dashboard renders a prominent unreconciled banner and disables the export control for that period, and `AnalyticsReconciliationFailed` has alerted the data team — figures are never silently served as authoritative.

### Edge Cases

* A credit note is issued against an invoice in an already-closed month — a dated adjustment row is posted to the current period and the closed month's reported figure is preserved, with the restatement visible in a restatements view.
* A `PaymentReceived` event is redelivered by JetStream — the `source_event_id` unique constraint makes it a no-op and collection efficiency does not double-count.

items.title: Clinical outcomes BI dashboard

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

The platform has no clinical outcomes reporting. MediCore emits `EncounterAdmitted`, `EncounterDischarged`, `DiagnosisRecorded` and `ProcedurePerformed` events onto NATS JetStream, and LabConnect emits `LabResultReady`, but nothing consumes them for quality measurement. A hospital administrator or quality manager who needs to know last month's inpatient mortality rate, average length of stay by specialty, or unplanned return-to-theatre rate has no answer other than manually tallying discharge summaries.

This blocks two things. Clinically, the medical superintendent and the hospital quality committee cannot run mortality and morbidity review with reliable denominators, so outliers in a specialty go unnoticed for months. Commercially, NABH accreditation requires a hospital to collect, trend and act on a defined set of quality indicators, and produce that evidence at assessment. A hospital that cannot generate indicator trends from its HMS will keep a parallel spreadsheet, which undermines the value of the platform and is a live objection in sales conversations.

The architectural rule that analytics never runs on the live clinical database (BRIEF §7) means this cannot be solved with reporting queries against MediCore. It needs a warehouse fed asynchronously, holding de-identified and aggregated data, with row-level security so no tenant can see another hospital's outcomes.

Affected roles: hospital administrator, medical superintendent, quality manager, department heads, and the DPO who must be satisfied that outcome reporting does not expose identifiable PHI without lawful basis under DPDP 2023.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** hospital quality manager
**I want** a clinical outcomes dashboard with trended indicators broken down by facility, ward, specialty and consultant
**So that** the quality committee can identify deteriorating outcomes early and evidence indicator trends at NABH assessment.

### Scope

**In scope**

* Analytics warehouse tables (`analytics.fact_encounter_outcome`, `analytics.dim_*`) populated from MediCore and LabConnect domain events via a Go consumer, with pseudonymised patient keys.
* Indicator computation for: inpatient mortality rate, average length of stay (ALOS), 30-day unplanned readmission rate, unplanned return to theatre, LAMA/DAMA rate, surgical site infection rate, and caesarean section rate.
* Denominator and numerator definitions stored as versioned indicator specifications, so a changed definition does not silently rewrite history.
* AdminConnect dashboard (Next.js 16) with trend charts, period-over-period comparison, and drill-down to facility → specialty → consultant.
* Filters: date range, facility, ward, specialty, admission type (elective/emergency), payer class.
* OpenFGA authorisation so consultant-level breakdowns are visible only to roles entitled to see them.
* CSV export of any displayed aggregate, with an audit record per export.

**Out of scope**

* Bed occupancy, turnover and capacity metrics — owned by #386.
* Revenue, payer mix and receivables — owned by #385.
* Predictive readmission scoring; this issue reports observed readmission rate only, the model is #387.
* The event ingestion transport and warehouse provisioning itself — assumed delivered by the Data Platform epic; this issue consumes it.
* Custom report builder and scheduled report delivery — separate stories in the Reporting epic.

---

## Recommended Solution

Build an `outcomes-analytics` Go module consuming a durable JetStream pull consumer on `medicore.encounter.*`, `medicore.procedure.*` and `labconnect.result.*`. The consumer writes to a separate analytics PostgreSQL 16 cluster — not the clinical database — and never calls back into MediCore.

**De-identification at the boundary.** The consumer replaces `patient_id` with `patient_pseudo_id`, an HMAC-SHA256 of the patient UUID keyed per tenant with a key held outside the analytics database. This keeps longitudinal linkage possible (essential for readmission denominators) without carrying a re-identifiable key into OLAP. No name, ABHA number, phone or address crosses the boundary.

**Data model** (analytics schema, all tables RLS-enabled on `tenant_id`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_encounter_outcome (
  encounter_key      bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  facility_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  patient_pseudo_id  bytea NOT NULL,
  admit_date_key     int  NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_date,
  discharge_date_key int  REFERENCES analytics.dim_date,
  specialty_key      int  NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_specialty,
  practitioner_key   int  REFERENCES analytics.dim_practitioner,
  ward_key           int  REFERENCES analytics.dim_ward,
  admission_type     text NOT NULL CHECK (admission_type IN ('elective','emergency','transfer')),
  discharge_disposition text CHECK (discharge_disposition IN
                         ('routine','lama','transferred','deceased','absconded')),
  los_hours          int,
  is_readmission_30d boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  index_encounter_key bigint REFERENCES analytics.fact_encounter_outcome,
  source_event_id    uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  ingested_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON analytics.fact_encounter_outcome
  (tenant_id, facility_id, discharge_date_key, specialty_key);
```

`source_event_id UNIQUE` makes ingestion idempotent under JetStream at-least-once redelivery.

Indicator definitions live in `analytics.indicator_spec (code, version, numerator_sql, denominator_sql, effective_from, effective_to)`. Aggregates are materialised nightly by a Temporal scheduled workflow into `analytics.agg_indicator_daily (tenant_id, facility_id, indicator_code, spec_version, grain_keys…, numerator, denominator, value)`. Storing `spec_version` on every aggregate row is what prevents a definition change from silently rewriting history — a new version backfills into new rows rather than mutating old ones.

Readmission linkage runs as a deferred pass: when a new admission lands, the workflow looks back 30 days on `patient_pseudo_id` within the same tenant and sets `is_readmission_30d` plus `index_encounter_key`. Because a readmission can only be known after the fact, the dashboard marks the trailing 30 days as provisional rather than showing an artificially low rate.

**API surface** (AdminConnect BFF, all tenant-scoped):

* `GET /api/v1/analytics/outcomes/indicators` — list available indicators and current spec version.
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/outcomes/series?indicator=&from=&to=&grain=&facility_id=&specialty_id=` — trended values.
* `GET /api/v1/analytics/outcomes/breakdown?indicator=&period=&dimension=specialty|ward|practitioner`
* `POST /api/v1/analytics/outcomes/exports` — creates a CSV export job, returns a signed time-limited object-storage URL.

**Events consumed:** `EncounterAdmitted`, `EncounterDischarged`, `ProcedurePerformed`, `DiagnosisRecorded`, `LabResultReady`. **Published:** `AnalyticsAggregateRefreshed` (so dashboards can invalidate cached tiles) and `AnalyticsExportRequested` (audit).

**OpenFGA model.** Consultant-attributed outcomes are sensitive — a mortality rate attributed to a named surgeon is a professional-standing matter. Model it explicitly:

```
type analytics_indicator
  relations
    define facility: [facility]
    define viewer_aggregate: quality_manager from facility or admin from facility
    define viewer_attributed: quality_manager from facility or medical_superintendent from facility
```

A department head gets `viewer_attributed` only for practitioners in their own department; everyone else sees the practitioner dimension suppressed rather than an error, so the dashboard degrades gracefully.

**Sequencing.** Depends on the Data Platform epic delivering the analytics cluster and JetStream stream retention, and on MediCore emitting discharge disposition on `EncounterDischarged` (raise a blocking dependency if the field is absent). #386 and #387 both build on `fact_encounter_outcome`, so the schema must land first.

**Risks.** Small-denominator cells make rates meaningless and can re-identify a patient — suppress any cell with denominator below a configurable threshold (default 11) and label it "suppressed (low volume)". Late-arriving events skew closed periods — aggregates are recomputed for a 7-day trailing window each night. Definition drift between hospitals is handled by versioned specs rather than per-tenant forks of the query code.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a tenant with 18 months of ingested encounter events across three facilities
**When** a quality manager opens the clinical outcomes dashboard, selects the last 12 months at monthly grain, and filters to the General Surgery specialty
**Then** ALOS, inpatient mortality rate and 30-day readmission rate render as monthly trend lines with numerator and denominator visible on hover, values match a direct query against `agg_indicator_daily` for the same spec version, and the page reaches interactive within the agreed threshold.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the analytics PostgreSQL cluster is unreachable
**When** a user requests an indicator series
**Then** the API returns `503` with a retry-after hint, the dashboard shows an explicit "outcome data temporarily unavailable" state naming the last successful refresh timestamp, no partial or zero-valued chart is rendered that could be mistaken for a real result, and the failure is recorded as an OpenTelemetry span error with the tenant and indicator code but no patient identifiers.

### Edge Cases

* A discharge event arrives for an encounter whose admission event was never received — the row is quarantined in `analytics.ingest_orphan` and excluded from denominators rather than defaulting `los_hours` to zero.
* The same `EncounterDischarged` event is redelivered by JetStream — the unique constraint on `source_event_id` makes the second write a no-op and the indicator value does not change.
* A specialty–month cell has a denominator of 4 — the value is suppressed and shown as "low volume", not as 0% or 100%.
* A user requests a period that predates the tenant's go-live — the chart renders only from first-data date with an explicit "no data before" boundary marker.
* A department head requests a practitioner breakdown covering consultants outside their department — out-of-department rows are omitted by the OpenFGA check, and the visible total is labelled as filtered so it is not read as a facility total.
* An indicator specification is superseded mid-period — the dashboard shows a version marker on the trend line at the changeover point instead of joining incomparable values into one continuous series.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.

items.title: Set up measuring limits for tokens
items.body:
As a billing and observability stakeholder for our AI-based email journey builder
I want the system to capture and log detailed token consumption metrics for every LLM response
So that we can support accurate billing, monitor rate limits (TPM/TPD), and comply with current usage and audit requirements for large-scale LLM applications.

**### Description**
We need a standardized, production-grade token usage logging capability across all LLM calls in the email journey builder platform.
​

For every model response, the platform must capture:

Per-request token usage (prompt, completion, total) as returned by the LLM provider.

Rolling **TPM** (tokens per minute) and **TPD** (tokens per day) metrics for rate-limit and quota monitoring aligned with provider tiers and usage policies.

Aggregated **total tokens** per:

User session (chat/journey-design session).

End customer (our tenant/customer account).

Global environment (for capacity and cost tracking).

These metrics must be logged in a structured, queryable way to support:

Accurate and auditable cost attribution per customer, feature, and environment.

Real-time and historical monitoring of rate limits (TPM/TPD/RPM/RPD) to avoid throttling and service disruption.

Downstream billing logic that can use token counts as a primary metric for usage-based pricing and reporting, in line with current industry standards for LLM-based billing.

Compliance/audit requirements by maintaining an immutable record of usage metadata for each interaction (without requiring storage of full raw content beyond existing policies).

### Functional Requirements
**Per-Response Usage Capture**

For every LLM API call (including retries), capture at minimum:

prompt_tokens

completion_tokens

total_tokens

Model identifier (e.g., gpt-4.1-mini, etc.).

Request timestamp (UTC).

Tenant/customer ID, user ID (where available), session/conversation ID, feature/context (e.g., “journey_builder_chat”).

**Rolling TPM Calculation**

Maintain an in-memory or fast-store rolling window of the last N minutes per:

API key / project / environment, and

Tenant/customer (if rate-limited separately).

For each new response, compute current TPM as sum of total_tokens in the last 60 seconds for that scope.

Expose the current TPM value in logs/metrics for observability and alerting.

**Daily TPD Calculation**

Maintain a running TPD counter per:

API key / project / environment,

Tenant/customer.

Reset counters at the start of each billing day (configurable timezone, default UTC).

Store TPD values in a way that supports reconciliation with provider dashboards and billing APIs.

**Session and Tenant Totals**

Track session-level token totals for each conversation/journey design session, from first to last message.

Track tenant-level cumulative tokens over configurable ranges (e.g., per day, per billing cycle).

These aggregates must be easily accessible for:

In-app analytics (e.g., “tokens used this month” per customer).

Back-office billing/export processes.

**Structured Logging & Storage**

Emit structured logs (e.g., JSON) per request with all token and context fields.

Ensure logs can be ingested by existing logging/observability stack (e.g., ELK, OpenTelemetry, Data Warehouse, or similar).
​

Design log/event schema to support long-term retention and compliance, including:

Retention controls.

PII-safe storage (no unnecessary sensitive content; IDs instead of raw text where possible).
​

**Rate Limit & Billing Alignment**

Align metric definitions (TPM, TPD, RPM/RPD) with the latest LLM provider documentation and tiers, so that we can:

Predict and prevent rate-limit breaches.

Attribute cost/capacity against provider-level quotas per model and tier.

Provide hooks for a future billing engine to:

Multiply token counts by model-specific price per 1K tokens.

Generate tenant-level usage and billing reports purely from these logs/metrics.

**Audit & Compliance Considerations**

Ensure logs are timestamped, immutable, and traceable to the originating user/session for audit trails (without violating data minimization principles).

Provide configuration for log retention periods to satisfy regulatory requirements (e.g., finance/enterprise customers who may require specific retention policies).
​

### Non-Functional Requirements
**Performance**: Token logging must add minimal overhead to response latency (target microseconds–low milliseconds per call). Aggregation (TPM/TPD) should be O(1) or close.

**Reliability**: Logging must be resilient to transient failures (e.g., non-blocking: a failed log write must not break the user-facing flow).

**Security & Privacy:**

Do not log raw prompt/response bodies in this feature beyond what’s already allowed by existing policies.

Ensure token logs do not include sensitive PII beyond IDs and necessary metadata.
​

Configurability: Ability to enable/disable or throttle detailed logging per environment (dev, staging, prod) and possibly per tenant.

### Acceptance Criteria
**Per-Response Logging**

Given any LLM response,

When the response is received by our backend,

Then a log entry is created containing prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens, model ID, timestamp, tenant ID, user ID (if available), and session ID.

**TPM Calculation**

Given a burst of requests from the same API key within 60 seconds,

When I query metrics/logs,

Then I see a correct TPM value equal to the sum of total_tokens for those requests in that minute, consistent with manual recomputation.

**TPD Calculation**

Given continuous usage across a full day,

When I query the daily token usage for a tenant or environment,

Then TPD equals the sum of total_tokens for all requests in that day and resets correctly at the defined day boundary.

**Session Totals**

Given a multi-turn chat session with 5+ messages,

When the session ends,

Then the session record shows the correct total tokens used across all turns.

**Tenant/Billing Readiness**

Given a tenant with usage over a billing period,

When I export or query their token usage,

Then I can derive model-level token totals per tenant and per period that reconcile (within known tolerances) with provider usage dashboards.

**Observability**

Given the system is under normal load,

When I open our observability dashboard,

Then I can view time-series charts of TPM/TPD and total tokens, filterable by environment and tenant.
​

**Resilience & Safety**

If the logging backend is temporarily unavailable,

Then the main user flow (LLM response to user) still succeeds, and logs are either buffered or safely dropped per design, without system crashes.

### Dependencies / Notes for OpenCode Integration
Use the existing LLM client wrapper (if present) as the single integration point to:

Read usage fields from provider responses.

Emit standardized log events and update in-memory counters.

Ensure OpenCode can identify:

The logging interface to extend.

The metric names/labels to use for TPM/TPD.

The JSON schema for log events.

If you share your current tech stack (e.g., Node/Java/Spring/Go, which logging/metrics stack you use), I can add a short “Implementation Notes” block tailored to that environment.


### Implementation Notes (Go)
**Language / Runtime**

- Go (1.21+ recommended to leverage the log/slog package for structured JSON logging).

​

**Logging Approach**

Use **structured logging** with log/slog (or an equivalent structured logger like Zap/Zerolog if already standardized in the codebase) to emit JSON logs containing all token metrics and context fields.

Configure a JSON handler for production so logs can be ingested by your existing log pipeline (e.g., ELK, Loki, Datadog, Grafana, etc.).

### Suggested Go Structure
**Central LLM Client Wrapper**

- Introduce or extend a shared LLM client wrapper (e.g., llm.Client) that all model calls go through.
- 
- This wrapper should be responsible for:

  - Calling the provider SDK/HTTP client.
  - 
  - Reading usage (prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens) from the response.
  - 
  - Invoking a TokenMetricsRecorder to update TPM/TPD and emit logs.

**TokenMetricsRecorder Interface**

```
go
type TokenUsage struct {
    PromptTokens    int
    CompletionTokens int
    TotalTokens     int
    Model           string
    TenantID        string
    UserID          string
    SessionID       string
    Feature         string // e.g. "journey_builder_chat"
    Timestamp       time.Time
}

type TokenMetricsRecorder interface {
    Record(usage TokenUsage)
}
In-Memory TPM/TPD Implementation (Thread-Safe)

Use a sync.Mutex-protected structure or sync.RWMutex plus per-key maps (e.g., keyed by tenantID and/or environment) to maintain sliding-window TPM and daily TPD.

go
type MetricsRecorder struct {
    mu          sync.Mutex
    tpmWindow   map[string][]TokenUsage   // key: scope (e.g. tenantID or env)
    dailyTotals map[string]int            // key: scope
    lastReset   time.Time
    logger      *slog.Logger
}
```

- Record should:
  
  - Append the new usage to the appropriate scope.
  
  - Prune entries older than 60s for TPM.
  
  - Sum TotalTokens for TPM.
  
  - Increment dailyTotals[scope] and reset when time.Now().UTC().Day() changes.
  
  - Emit a structured log entry with:
  
      - Per-response usage and calculated current_tpm, current_tpd, session_total (if available), tenant_total.

**Example Record Implementation (Sketch)**

```
go
func (r *MetricsRecorder) Record(u TokenUsage) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()

    scope := u.TenantID
    if scope == "" {
        scope = "global"
    }

    // Reset daily totals on day change (UTC)
    now := u.Timestamp
    if r.lastReset.IsZero() || now.UTC().Day() != r.lastReset.UTC().Day() {
        r.dailyTotals = make(map[string]int)
        r.lastReset = now
    }

    // Initialize maps
    if r.tpmWindow == nil {
        r.tpmWindow = make(map[string][]TokenUsage)
    }
    if r.dailyTotals == nil {
        r.dailyTotals = make(map[string]int)
    }

    // Append to TPM window
    window := append(r.tpmWindow[scope], u)

    // Prune older than 60 seconds
    cutoff := now.Add(-60 * time.Second)
    pruned := window[:0]
    tpm := 0
    for _, w := range window {
        if w.Timestamp.After(cutoff) {
            pruned = append(pruned, w)
            tpm += w.TotalTokens
        }
    }
    r.tpmWindow[scope] = pruned

    // Update TPD
    r.dailyTotals[scope] += u.TotalTokens
    tpd := r.dailyTotals[scope]

    // Emit structured log
    r.logger.Info("llm_token_usage",
        slog.String("tenant_id", u.TenantID),
        slog.String("user_id", u.UserID),
        slog.String("session_id", u.SessionID),
        slog.String("feature", u.Feature),
        slog.String("model", u.Model),
        slog.Time("timestamp", u.Timestamp),
        slog.Int("prompt_tokens", u.PromptTokens),
        slog.Int("completion_tokens", u.CompletionTokens),
        slog.Int("total_tokens", u.TotalTokens),
        slog.Int("tpm", tpm),
        slog.Int("tpd", tpd),
    )
}
```
**Integration with Observability / OTel (Optional but Recommended)**

- In addition to logs, emit metrics via OpenTelemetry for Go, such as:
- 
    - llm_tokens_total (counter).
    - llm_tokens_tpm (gauge or windowed counter).
    - Labels: tenant_id, model, feature, env.
     
- Correlate logs with traces (span IDs in logs) if you already use OTel tracing, to tie LLM usage to user requests and workflows.


**Billing / Export Layer**

Provide a simple Go service or job that queries your log sink or metrics backend and aggregates token counts per tenant and period, mapping to pricing (e.g., cost = tokens / 1000 × model_rate).

Ensure export is deterministic and can be reconciled with provider usage APIs and dashboards.
